A choropleth shades each region by a value — emissions, incidence, turnout, income. It is the most
common map in data analysis and the easiest to get *subtly wrong*: most "my map is all one colour"
complaints are not rendering bugs but scale bugs. Here we build a choropleth in Python with
[canvasxpress](https://pypi.org/project/canvasxpress/) that stays vivid and honest on exactly the
kind of heavy-tailed data that flattens naive maps. The join and the colouring happen inside the
render, so every figure is one portable spec you can re-run from Python, R or the browser.

## Install

```bash
pip install canvasxpress pandas
```

## First, the trap: colour encodes a *rate*, not a *count*

A choropleth fills an **area**, and area is a size channel your eye cannot help reading. Shade
regions by a raw count — total cases, total emissions, total sales — and big, populous regions light
up simply because they are big and populous. You have drawn a population map with extra steps.

The fix is almost always to map a **rate or density**: cases per 100k, emissions per capita, sales
per store. Reserve raw counts for a *proportional-symbol* map (a sized bubble at each centroid),
where the size channel carries the count honestly. Decide which question you are answering before
you pick the geometry — this one choice prevents most misleading maps.

## One value per region

A choropleth needs exactly one measurement per shape. In canvasxpress the **columns** (`smps`) are
the regions — they match the map by name — and each **row** (`vars`) is a variable you can colour by.
Here it's CO₂ emissions per country for 2018. We load a prepared table; swap it for your own (any
`country → value` table works).

```{python}
import pandas as pd

dat = pd.read_csv(
    "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt",
    sep="\t", index_col=0,
)
smp = pd.read_csv(
    "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt",
    sep="\t", index_col=0,
).reindex(dat.columns)        # align annotation to the country order

print(dat.shape)              # (1, N): one row (CO2) x N countries
dat.iloc[:, :4]
```

## The map: quantile classes on a viridis ramp

`y` carries the matrix (`vars` = the variable, `smps` = the countries, `data` = the values); the
optional `x` block adds per-country annotations (continent, ISO code) for richer tooltips. The two
choices that make this map *work* are in the colour scale: a seven-stop viridis `colorSpectrum`,
and `colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "quantile"`, which puts an equal number of countries in every
colour class. On skewed data that guarantee is what keeps all seven colours on the map.

```{python}
from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {
        "vars": list(dat.index),            # ["CO2"]
        "smps": list(dat.columns),          # country names
        "data": dat.values.tolist(),        # [[values]]
    },
    "x": {
        "Continent": smp["Continent"].tolist(),
        "Code":      smp["Code"].tolist(),
    },
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Map",
    "colorBy":   "CO2",
    "topoJSON":  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
    "mapId":     "co2Quantile",
    "colorSpectrum": ["#440154", "#443983", "#31688e", "#21918c",
                      "#35b779", "#90d743", "#fde725"],
    "colorSpectrumBreaksMethod": "quantile",
    "mapColor":        "#d9dde3",
    "mapOutlineColor": "#ffffff",
    "legendPosition":  "bottom",
    "title":    "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
    "subtitle": "Seven quantile classes: each colour holds about 28 of 198 countries",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="co2quant", data=data, config=config, width=760, height=520)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)
```

Every band of the ramp is doing work: the darkest purples are the smallest emitters, the yellows the
largest, and the legend's break values tell you the class edges are *data-driven*, not evenly spaced.
Hover any country for its name, continent and value.

## Why not just a plain linear ramp?

Because the data is **heavy-tailed** — a few countries emit thousands of megatonnes while most emit
almost nothing. On a linear scale, **195 of these 198 countries fall into the bottom fifth of the
range**, so a continuous ramp paints nearly the whole world one pale tone and spends its colour on
two or three outliers:

```{python}
linear = {
    "graphType": "Map",
    "colorBy":   "CO2",
    "topoJSON":  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
    "mapId":     "co2Linear",
    "legendPosition": "left",
    "theme": "solarized",
    "title":    "The same data on a plain linear ramp",
    "subtitle": "195 of 198 countries sit in the bottom fifth of the scale - the map goes flat",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="co2lin", data=data, config=linear, width=700, height=480)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)
```

This is the single most common choropleth failure. The cure is **classing**:

- `"colorSpectrumBreaksMethod": "quantile"` — equal *counts* per class. Every colour is used, by
  construction. The right default for skewed data and for "which regions rank high/low" questions.
- `"colorSpectrumBreaksMethod": "jenks"` — natural breaks that minimise within-class variance. Best
  when the data has genuine clusters with gaps between them; on smoothly heavy-tailed data like this
  it piles almost everything into the bottom class, so check the legend before you trust it.
- Three to seven classes is the usable range — beyond that, readers cannot match colours to the
  legend.

## Choose the palette on purpose

The palette is the scale's grammar, not decoration:

- **Sequential** (dark → light of ordered hues, like viridis above) for a quantity that only goes
  up: counts, rates, concentrations.
- **Diverging** (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful *above and below
  a reference*: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Give a three-colour
  `colorSpectrum` and pin the midpoint with `colorSpectrumZeroValue`:

  ```python
  "colorBy": "Change",
  "colorSpectrum": ["#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"],  # blue - neutral - red
  "colorSpectrumZeroValue": 0,                          # value mapped to the middle colour
  ```

  Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a
  "normal" the data does not have.

Viridis and the ColorBrewer ramps are colour-blind-safe and perceptually ordered; a rainbow ramp is
neither, so readers cannot tell which end means "more". Keep the *same* scale across small multiples
so maps stay comparable.

## Polish: legend, labels and base styling

- `subtitle` / `source` — caption units and provenance.
- `"legendNumberFormat": {"style": "decimal", "decimals": 1, "suffix": "%"}` — format legend ticks.
- `mapColor` / `mapOutlineColor` — the fill for **no-data** regions (a neutral grey) and the shape
  borders, so missing data reads as missing rather than as a value.
- `"showMapLabels": True` — draw region names (best on few-region maps; clutters a world map).
- `"legendInside": True` — float the legend over empty ocean to reclaim width.

## Beyond the world map

- **Other boundaries.** Point `topoJSON` at any shape file — US states, a country's provinces,
  counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
- **Projection.** `"mapProjection": "albers"` (equal-area) or `"mercator"`. Equal-area projections
  matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes and exaggerates their visual weight.
- **Categorical maps.** Point `colorBy` at a categorical column for a qualitative choropleth with a
  discrete legend.
- **Markers.** Add `decorations` to drop labelled points on cities or call out specific regions.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — is one portable spec you can store,
validate and re-render from R or JavaScript.
